member.name: T:OpenIGI.UI.Animation.Spring
member.summary: A critically-damped spring that chases a moving target, carrying velocity so it settles smoothly rather than restarting on every change.

remarks.para: Where a plays a fixed curve to a fixed target, a spring is the right tool when the target itself keeps moving — a value tracking the mouse, a carousel following a flung gesture, a focus ring chasing a selection that the player is scrubbing through. It never overshoots (it is critically damped) and it is framerate-independent.

The integrator is the closed-form critically-damped step from Game Programming Gems 4 (Thomas Lowe's "smooth damp"): stable for any time step and any smooth time, so a long stall between frames eases in correctly instead of exploding the way a naive Euler spring would. Advance it with a real elapsed time delta, never a simulation tick — the same rule every other animation here follows.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.UI.Focus.FocusManager
member.summary: Tracks which widget holds focus and moves it by directional traversal — the one model that mouse, keyboard and gamepad all drive.

remarks.para: Directional traversal is spatial, not order-based: pressing a direction moves focus to the nearest focusable widget that lies that way, measured from the current one. That is what lets a gamepad reach a grid of cards or a two-column settings form as naturally as it reaches a single list, and it is why the model is shared — the mouse sets focus by pointing, the keyboard and pad by pressing a direction, but there is only ever one focused widget and one way it looks focused.

Scoring favours candidates directly ahead: the cost is the distance travelled in the pressed direction plus twice the sideways offset, so a widget dead ahead beats one that is nearer but off to the side. Widgets are gathered fresh from the tree each move, so the traversal always reflects the current layout — collapsed or disabled widgets simply are not candidates.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.UI.Layout.LayoutContext
member.summary: The mapping from the interface's authored coordinate space to the back buffer it is drawn into.

remarks.para: Why a reference resolution. Every screen is authored once against a 16:9 reference (1920×1080 by default): a button is "220 units wide", a title is "64 units tall", spacing is "24 units". Those numbers never change. What changes per display is , the number of back-buffer pixels one authored unit becomes. This is the same idea as the retail UI's whole-number , generalised to a continuous factor because the modern shell is vector-and-SDF rather than pixel art and does not need to snap to integers.

Why it is correct from 4:3 to 32:9. Two things vary independently. Authored sizes (fonts, paddings, widget extents) are multiplied by , so a button keeps the same visual proportion of the screen at every aspect ratio. Authored positions are resolved by anchoring against — the whole usable viewport — so a full-bleed background covers a 32:9 monitor and an edge-pinned HUD element stays pinned, while a centred menu column stays centred. member.summary: Persists a rasterised to disk so the stb_truetype pass is paid once rather than on every launch.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.UI.UiPainter
member.content: Bands of a ring -- arcs with a thickness -- filled with edges smoothed all round.
member.summary: The interface's drawing surface: rectangles, polygons, gradients, sprites, frosted glass and text, emitted through an with clip, opacity and transform stacks.

remarks.para: One painter serves every backend. The game hands it a renderer over its sprite batch, so UI draws interleave with the HUD and the console in submission order exactly as the original's painter's algorithm expects; the launcher hands it a renderer over a Skia canvas. Everything that should look the same on both — clipping, edge feathering, gradients, text layout — happens here, and the renderer only puts the resulting device-space quads and glyphs on screen.

Clipping is done on the CPU. A clip rectangle is applied by trimming each rectangle to it and adjusting its texture coordinates in proportion, and each polygon by Sutherland–Hodgman. That is enough for axis-aligned UI: a scroll view pushes a clip, its rows draw trimmed, and it pops. It keeps renderers free of scissor state, and it is what lets the draw output be asserted through a recording renderer without a GPU.

member.content: Strokes and dots with every edge smoothed, for fine marks that sit off the pixel grid: an aiming mark, a tick.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.UI.UiSurfaces
member.summary: The small generated texture that gives the interface rounded corners and soft shadows.

remarks.para: Why this exists. can fill axis-aligned rectangles, draw textured quads and draw text. It has no rounded-rectangle primitive, no line, and no blur — and a modern floating window needs a soft corner and a shadow under it or it reads as a debug overlay from 1999. Both shapes are radially symmetric, so a single quadrant of each, mirrored into four corners and stretched along the straight edges, is enough to draw either at any size.

It is generated rather than shipped: it is a few thousand operations once at start-up, it never needs an artist, and it cannot go missing from an install. There is deliberately no disk cache — the font atlases are the expensive thing and already have one; caching this would cost more in file handling than it saves.
Both shapes live in the alpha channel over white, so a draw modulates them with a vertex colour exactly as text does. One texture, two sprites, nine quads per rounded figure.

member.summary: Continues each quadrant's solid inside past its edge, so filtering never samples off the shape.
member.param: The quadrant's left edge in the atlas.

remarks.para: A quadrant is authored with the shape's outside at its top-left and its solid inside at the bottom-right, and a draw samples right up to that inside edge. Bilinear filtering there reaches one texel further, which without this lands in the empty atlas between the quadrants and halves the alpha along the seam.

It goes unnoticed for an ordinary rounded panel, whose corners meet stretched edge strips carrying the same solid value. A figure whose radius is half its height — a circle, a capsule — has no edge strips at all: its four corners meet each other, and the seam draws a faint cross through the middle of the shape. Half the guard band is left clear so the neighbouring quadrant's own outside edge still filters into nothing.

member.summary: A viewport onto a single taller child, scrolled vertically, its content clipped to the viewport and a thumb shown when there is more than fits.

The content is measured with unbounded height and arranged offset upwards by the scroll amount; the viewport clips it (on the CPU, see ). A spring carries the visible offset so a page jump glides rather than snapping. This is the console scrollback's viewport and, in the shell, a long settings panel's.

member.summary: A scrolling list of uniform-height rows that measures, arranges and draws only the rows actually on screen.

remarks.para: Why not . That viewport measures and arranges a single child at unbounded height. Giving it a stack of four thousand labels would measure and arrange four thousand elements every frame to show twenty of them — in a tool whose whole purpose is to report the frame budget it was quietly eating.

The trade is that rows are not elements. A row draws through a callback, so it has no identity, no focus and no animation of its own. For a log or a variable table that is the right trade: the rows are data, they are numerous, and they are replaced wholesale. Anything that needs per-row state belongs in a real widget in a .

The scroll offset is carried by a , so a page jump glides in the same way the rest of the interface does, while the row range is computed from the settled target rather than the animated value — otherwise rows would pop in and out during the glide.

member.summary: Hosts floating s: arranges each into its own pixel frame, keeps them in a front-to-back order, and owns the one drag or resize that can be in flight.

The mouse's frame deltas are zeroed while input is captured — and a console that has taken the keyboard has captured it — whereas its position keeps being reported precisely so a shell can use it. Dragging is therefore resolved against the position the grab began at.

member.remarks: Visibility is settled here, at the start of the measure pass, not during arrange. returns immediately for a collapsed element without measuring its content, and throws for anything that was never measured. Deciding visibility in the later pass therefore left a window opened this frame still carrying last frame's collapsed flag while it was measured, so its content was skipped and then arranged — which is a crash on the first frame any panel is shown, and only that frame.
